blindSummary:
This state/province carried a state/province-level "LGBT-free" resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under supranational funding pressure. One of its towns (population ~40,000) was the first local authority in the country to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to the national capital's LGBT+ charter signed a month earlier; the town became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as elsewhere in the country's conservative-region belt the repeal was coerced rather than a change of conviction — the underlying civic mobilisation that produced the country's first anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the state/province scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.
blindSourceSummaries: Social-science institute publication on the country's LGBT-free zones: a town in this state/province's capital county (~40,000 people) became the country's first 'LGBT-free' municipality in March 2019, a non-binding resolution against 'homosexual propaganda' and 'LGBT ideology' that withdrew support for equality organisations - explicitly framed by its deputy council chair as opposition to the capital's February 2019 LGBT+ charter; with backing from the governing conservative party and senior clergy, over 80 municipalities and four regional authorities had similar declarations by March 2020, mapped by an activists' hate-atlas project and lobbied for by a conservative legal institute.

LGBTQ+ news report (September 2021): under direct funding pressure from the supranational body, this state/province repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021 alongside two siblings, joining an earlier wave - the funding demands, not changed conviction, drove the rescissions.

Legal-overview article on the rise and fall of the country's LGBT-free zones: between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 local governments adopted 'LGBT ideology'-free resolutions or family-rights charters drafted by a conservative legal institute, covering about a third of the country at the movement's peak; the documents created no criminal penalties but symbolically sidelined LGBT residents from civic life; litigation by the national human-rights commissioner led courts to strike them down as unconstitutional, a supranational funding body threatened to freeze billions in regional funds, and the last remaining zone was abolished in spring 2025.
blindTangential: The resolution history targeted 'LGBT ideology' broadly rather than trans status specifically; with the document repealed, no formal instrument remains, but the mobilisation that produced the country's first anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto general-hostility signal.
